verses.1: Al-Mizan explains that the opening oath has the omitted conclusion that people will be resurrected. It records competing readings of al-nāziʿāt as angels drawing out souls—either generally or those of disbelievers—death itself, stars moving between horizons, drawn bows or soldiers, and animals drawn to pasture. Gharqan, an unqualified maṣdar, intensifies the action as severe or complete seizing. An editor notes that the commentary later rejects these proposals as discordant with 79:5 and reads the five oaths as stages in angels’ direction of affairs.
verses.2: Al-Mizan notes that nashṭ can mean drawing or absorbing easily, emerging or bringing out gently, or untying a knot. Accordingly, exegetes have identified those who discharge gently with angels drawing out souls generally, angels gently drawing believers’ souls, angels forcibly drawing disbelievers’ souls, believers’ souls themselves, stars changing horizons, arrows leaving bows, death drawing souls out, or animals leaving one region for another. An editor clarifies that the bow is the object of drawing whereas soldiers are its agents, and that the believers’-souls reading rests on the intransitive sense.
verses.3: Al-Mizan lists readings of sabḥan, whose basic sense is swift movement: angels may carry believers’ souls to paradise and disbelievers’ souls to hell, gently release believers’ souls to rest like something buoyant, or descend swiftly from heaven. Other proposals identify the oath with orbiting stars, galloping warhorses, deaths moving through animal souls, ships, clouds, or sea creatures. It notes that a swift horse is called sābiḥ and silently corrects the extracted word to ‘float’ for the watery comparisons.
verses.4: Al-Mizan reports several identifications of those who hasten with haste: angels surpassing humans in virtue, faith, and righteous action; angels of death rushing souls to paradise or hell; angels who take believers to paradise; revelation-angels outrunning devils; or believers’ souls hastening to the angels because they long to meet God. Further lexical proposals are stars, soldiers’ horses, and deaths overtaking human hopes. An editor explains that the plural ‘deaths’ denotes different modes or causes of dying.
verses.5: Al-Mizan says the five oaths share one context and an omitted conclusion—resurrection—so readings that make each oath a different object lack contextual evidence and conflict with the sūrah’s resurrection theme. It therefore identifies them with angels acting under God’s leave: the first two mark their forceful departure from the station of receiving the command; they then descend swiftly, race to their assignment, and direct the affair entrusted to them. The successive fāʾs make (79:3-5) a connected sequence, and the unqualified tadbīr in (79:5) concerns the world’s management; amran may specify the direction or be its object. This reading, which some traditions confirm, distinguishes this sūrah’s general angels of worldly direction from the revelation-angels in the openings of Sūrah al-Ṣāfiāt and Sūrah al-Mursalāt. Al-Mizan further treats angels as intermediaries between God and beings in return, legislation (tashrīʿ), and worldly governance. They administer death, resurrection and judgment; convey and protect revelation, assist messengers and believers; and execute divine command in the world. Their action is regular, hierarchically ordered, and never independent: superior angels convey God’s command to subordinates. Angelic and material causes are vertically related, not rival horizontal causes; an angel can cause the material cause while all causality remains traceable to God. Thus this rejects the polytheistic idea that God delegated independent control to archangels. An editor characterizes the illustration of incomplete causes requiring divine approval as an ‘intermediate and dualistic metaphysics.’
verses.6: Al-Mizan takes al-rājifah and al-rādifah as the first and following blows of the Trumpet: the former may be a tremulous, booming shake or the force that shakes the earth and mountains, and the latter what follows it. It finds less apparent the reading that the earth itself quakes first and the heavens and stars are then demolished. The unspoken complement of the preceding oaths—resurrection—heightens its enormity, and ‘the day’ fixes its time; the alternative that it merely supplies the temporal setting for the trembling hearts of 79:8 is judged unapparent.

verses.8: Al-Mizan reads the indefinite ‘hearts’ as indicating diverse conditions, with some hearts trembling in agitation on that day. It treats this as an independent statement describing that day. ‘Their looks’ refers back to those hearts because, where cognition, fear, and hope are attributed to the heart, the intended reality is the human soul; the eyes are specified because inward humility shows in them especially clearly. An editor notes that the plurality allows some, rather than all, hearts to be trembling.

verses.10: Al-Mizan understands the disbelievers’ question as their present-world skepticism about resurrection: al-ḥāfirah means an original or former state, so they incredulously ask whether death will restore them to life. This links those future trembling hearts and humbled eyes with the people who deny resurrection now. It rejects the proposal that al-ḥāfirah means the grave, though an editor observes that its grammatical objection is not decisive and that the reading can be construed plausibly. The alternative that they say this after being raised, in astonishment, is possible in itself but conflicts with the apparent context.
verses.11: Al-Mizan says the question about being crumbled bones repeats and sharpens the preceding skeptical question: if return after death seems unlikely, it appears still less likely after bones decay and bodily organs disintegrate. Nakhirah means decay or decomposition.
verses.12: Al-Mizan takes ‘that’ to refer to the implied return to life and explains karrah as return or recurrence. Calling it khāsirah either transfers loss figuratively from those returned to the return itself, or means a return characterized by loss. If (79:10-11) report their worldly belief, the statement is a derisive denial; its past tense clarifies that the preceding present tense concerns their current condition. If those verses instead describe their resurrection, it voices their regret and disappointment then.
verses.13: Al-Mizan answers the alleged difficulty of resurrection by saying that their return—or, on one proposal, the second Trumpet-blast—will require only one zajrah, a cry that drives them from death to life and from beneath the earth onto it. Fa-idhā conveys the suddenness of their appearing on al-sāhirah, a level, barren plain. It compares this effortless revival to the Hour’s coming in the twinkling of an eye, or faster (16:77).

verses.15: Al-Mizan introduces the ensuing Moses–Pharaoh narrative as a warning to polytheists who deny the afterlife and therefore reject religion, and as consolation to the Prophet. Pharaoh’s destruction demonstrates Moses’ true mission, God’s lordship over humankind, and the falsehood of the polytheistic notion that lower lords, rather than God, rule people; it therefore supports resurrection and retribution. ‘Has the story of Moses reached you?’ is a persuasive question that turns the Prophet’s attention to a consoling story while leaving deniers no excuse, not a request for information. The question works even if its audience already knows the story, so the passage leaves open whether this was its first Qur’anic telling; it notes prior references in 73:15-16, 7:103-171, and 20:9-97.
verses.16: Al-Mizan identifies Ṭuwá as the holy valley in which Moses first received revelation and was appointed a messenger. God’s command to go to Pharaoh is itself the explication of that call, without requiring an omitted ‘say’ or interpretive an; Pharaoh’s transgression explains the command. Moses then invites him to tazakkī, self-purification from transgression. Although the wording is literally incomplete, ilá (‘to’) shows that it asks whether Pharaoh has willingness or inclination for that purification.

verses.19: Al-Mizan says that guiding Pharaoh to his Lord means teaching him to know God, a knowledge that produces awe and restrains violations of servitude, as in (35:28). It offers two relations between the invitation and fear: tazakkī may be repentance and return to God, followed by faith-born fear that prevents disobedience; or it may itself be purification through obedience and avoidance of sin, with the following clause interpretively explaining it. An editor distinguishes the first as cure and the second as prevention.
verses.20: Al-Mizan reads fāʾ al-faṣīḥah as revealing an omitted sequence: Moses went to Pharaoh, called him, and then showed him the greatest sign. In light of the fuller Qur’anic accounts, it identifies that sign with the staff miracle, rather than all the miracles shown to Pharaoh and his elite. An editor explains that this fāʾ implies a contextually inferable omitted protasis and intensifies the speech’s concision.
verses.21: Al-Mizan says Pharaoh rejected Moses and his mission, called him a sorcerer, and disobeyed either Moses’ commands or God.
verses.22: Al-Mizan glosses idbār as turning away and saʿy as striving: Pharaoh turned back and exerted himself to oppose Moses and refute his message.
verses.23: Al-Mizan says Pharaoh forcibly mustered people from throughout his kingdom and then proclaimed, a sequence indicated by the following fāʾ; this supports his claim to lordship over all Egypt, not merely one group. It finds no evidence that the mustering was only of magicians. His claim, ‘I am your highest lord,’ apparently places him above the other gods accepted by his idolatrous people, not above merely human officials. The commentary infers that Pharaoh himself worshiped idols from (7:127), and suggests that he claimed superiority because he controlled livelihoods, order, and national glory while those gods did not. It rejects the rival monarch-only reading as contrary both to the verse’s apparent meaning and to Pharaoh’s claims in (28:38) and (26:29).

verses.25: Al-Mizan calls God’s ‘seizing’ an indirect expression for punishment and nakāl a punishment that deters those who witness or hear of it from earning its like. It therefore reads Pharaoh’s exemplary punishment ‘of the last and the first’ as punishment in the hereafter and this world: after death, and drowning with his hosts, respectively. An editor says the eternal punishment is named first for greater gravity and to preserve rhyme. The alternatives—punishment for his final and earlier lordship claims, his initial and final disobedience, or all earlier and later sins—are not quite apparent.
verses.26: Al-Mizan takes ‘that’ to mean the Moses narrative and reads the omitted object of khashyah broadly: it is a lesson for anyone with caution, since an intact human fiṭrah instinctively fears punishment and misery. It regards ‘one who fears God’ as a less expressive alternative.
verses.27: Al-Mizan addresses the polytheists’ derision of resurrection by asking whether they are more prodigious in creation than the sky, whose creation God elaborately describes through 79:33. The rhetorical question censures their skepticism: God who made what is far greater can recreate them in another realm. The argument also establishes resurrection’s necessity, not merely its possibility. God’s governance of the universe, including humankind, entails His lordship; that lordship entails prophethood and religious obligation, which require retribution at resurrection. ‘He built it’ begins the detailed confirmation that the sky is the more prodigious creation.
verses.28: Al-Mizan defines samk as a thing’s roof or upper part, and taswiyah as arranging and placing a thing’s constituents in their proper places according to a wise plan. It thus reads the verse as God raising the sky’s vault and fashioning it, with the latter sense illustrated by (15:29, 38:72).
verses.29: Al-Mizan says God darkened the night and manifested the day. Although ḍuḥá originally means the spreading of sunlight and extension of daytime, here it denotes the whole day because it contrasts with night. Night and day are ascribed to the sky through their heavenly cause—the appearance and disappearance of luminous bodies—and apply not only to earth but to any dark heavenly body illuminated by another.
verses.30:
Al-Mizan reads daḥāhā as God’s spreading or rolling out the earth after building and proportioning the sky, darkening its night, and brightening its day; it notes the proposed sense ‘with that’ for baʿd but refers the apparent Qur’anic account of creation to its discussion of 41:11. Bringing forth the earth’s water means springs and rivers, and its marʿá means plants generally, nourishing humans as well as animals, despite other possible lexical senses of pasture, grazing, time, or place. God made mountains firm to stabilize the earth and store water and minerals.

The resulting sky and earth are an enjoyment for people and livestock, which are made subservient to human benefit. For Al-Mizan, this beneficent, ordered creation obliges people to know, fear, and thank their Lord, and therefore requires recompense for good and evil. Since it is far greater than human creation, it also removes any warrant for regarding a second creation as difficult or improbable for God.

verses.34: Al-Mizan explains al-ṭāmmah as an overwhelming, indeflectible calamity; the resurrection is the Greatest Catastrophe because it surmounts every other disaster. The opening fāʾ makes its occurrence a necessary consequence of the creation and ordered direction of heaven and earth. The day it occurs, people remember their saʿy, their hard work, and hell is made visible to anyone capable of sight as its veil is removed. This, the commentary says, shows that hell already exists before resurrection; (50:22) is comparable though more comprehensive.

verses.37:
Al-Mizan supplies the implied result of the Greatest Catastrophe: people are divided into the two contrasted triads of hell’s dwellers and paradise’s inhabitants. Hell is for the one who commits tughyān—violating the limits of servitude in arrogant disregard of the Lord’s station—and prefers worldly adornment, which is following the ego and desire against God. Paradise is for the one who has khawf before the Lord’s station and restrains the soul from desire. Khawf is the awe and humility of the weak before the overpowering; the contrast means that Godwariness entails not inclining to worldly life and curbing desire.

The commentary stresses that the verse says to forbid the soul from evil, not that human beings never commit it: minor, un-defiant lapses fall within God’s expansive forgiveness, as in (53:31-32) and (4:31). It accordingly identifies the two poles as disbelief and sin versus belief and taqwá (Godwariness, self-restraint, piety), but leaves intermediate groups, including al-mustaḍʿafūn and people who mix good with evil, to God’s decision, forgiveness, intercession, or other means.

Al-Mizan reads the Lord’s maqām not as a standing-place before judgment or an empty supplementary word, but as the quality of His Lordship: omniscience, omnipotence, dominion, invincibility, mercy, and wrath. It is mercy and forgiveness for believers who restrain themselves, and painful chastisement for deniers and disobedient people. The alternatives require an unsupported omission or treat maqām as zāʾidah; editors identify that latter technical claim and the former objection explicitly.

verses.42: Al-Mizan says the present tense indicates the polytheists’ repeated, insistent demand that the Prophet fix the Hour’s time. Mursāhā, from a maṣdar meaning establishment or settlement, explains their derisive question: when will the denied Hour be established—that is, when will resurrection occur?
verses.43:
Al-Mizan treats the rhetorical question in (79:43) as negating the Prophet’s ability to know the Hour’s time. One reading takes dhikrá as emphatic frequent mention: min means ‘by means of,’ so repeated mention cannot yield its time, and the preposition signals a wide distance between the Prophet and such knowledge. It considers more plausible that dhikrá means mindfulness of a thing’s reality: he is not in a position to know the Hour’s reality and properties, and therefore its time.

The commentary reports but finds contextually contrived the readings that the time is outside his mission because he is only a warner, that his nearness to the Hour as Seal of the Prophets is itself the relevant reminder—supported by a Prophetic hadith—or that the verse continues the polytheists’ question. An editor, however, explicitly calls the mission-and-warmer reading the most apparent and contextually confirmed, taking dhikrá as notifying people of the time.
verses.44:
Al-Mizan says (79:44) explains why the Prophet cannot mention the Hour’s time: its reality, properties, and specific time belong only to his Lord, so people should not ask the Prophet and he cannot answer. It then tentatively offers a deeper justification: the Hour coincides with the annihilation of all things and apparent means, when all sovereignty belongs to Allah, the One, the All-Paramount (40:16). It is therefore directly ascribed to God with no real intermediate causal link, including time, and may not have a time in the real sense.

On that possibility, the Qur’an defines it through the extinction of this world, as in (39:68); descriptions involving earthly duration are metaphorical or analogical, including (79:46), (46:35), and (30:55), while (30:56) states the reality. Its suddenness is also affirmed in (7:187). Al-Mizan calls this profound and says reconciling it with other resurrection verses requires reflection, particularly on (50:22), while seeking God’s help.
verses.45: Al-Mizan says the Prophet is charged to warn those able to fear the Hour, not to disclose when it will occur. The exclusiveness of innamā is relative: calling him ‘only a warner’ negates knowledge of the Hour and the role of determining it for questioners. In context, fear means the receptivity and propensity to be apprehensive when reminded of the Hour, even before actual fear has arisen.
verses.46: Al-Mizan reads the comparison as portraying the Hour’s nearness: when people see it, the interval after their worldly life will seem no more than an evening or its forenoon. Their ‘stay’ is therefore the period in the grave between life and resurrection, measured against their whole worldly life. It rejects the view that this interval begins with their earlier inquiry about the Hour, since the statement is made after resurrection and other verses concern their pre-resurrection stay, including (23:112). It also judges weak the reading that ‘stay’ means their entire worldly life.
